text.p: Australian spending on overseas minerals and petroleum exploration rose 13 percent to A$486 million in fiscal 1995/96 (July-June) from the previous year, government figures released on Monday show.
Expenditure on petroleum exploration of A$318 million accounted for 65 percent of total overseas expenditure in 1995/96, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said.
Gold exploration was the next largest, with A$101 million, or 21 percent of the total spent in the 12 month period, the ABS said.
Exploration for base metals cost Australian companies A$38 million in 1995/96, or eight percent of the total for the year, the ABS said.
North America was the favoured destination for Australian explorers, who spent A$136 million in the region in 1995/96, the ABS said.
"This represents an increase of 53 percent on expenditure on this region in 1994/95," it said.
Exploration spending was also up in Indonesia, Latin America, Papua New Guinea and elsewhere in Asia, the ABS said.
Expenditure in Africa remained steady, while in Chile it dropped to A$2 million, less than 10 percent of the expenditure in the previous year, the ABS said.
For all of 1995/96, domestic spending on exploration, excluding petroleum, rose to A$960.2 million, of which A$547.1 million was spend looking for gold, from A$893.3 million.
Total domestic spending on petroleum exploration rose to A$752.2 million in 1995/96 from A$682.4 million the previous year, ABS figures show.
Total exploration spending at home for the quarter ended September 30, 1996 was A$274 million, down A$11 million from the previous quarter but A$47 million higher than a year earlier.
Total spending on domestic petroleum exploration was A$207 million in the quarter to September 30, 1996, up A$35 million, or 20 percent from the previous quarter, ABS figures show.

Onshore exploration for petroleum rose A$19 million, or 44 percent to A$61 million, while offshore exploration spending rose A$16 million, or 13 percent, to A$146 million in the September quarter, the ABS said.
